content: Neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia is a prevalent condition that poses a risk of neurotoxicity. In some cases, affected infants may develop bilirubin encephalopathy or kernicterus, which can result in long-term disabilities. Phototherapy is the primary treatment for neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia. As an adjunct to phototherapy, fluid supplementation has been proposed as a method to lower serum bilirubin levels. The proposed mechanisms include the dilutional effects of intravenous (IV) fluids or the enhancement of peristalsis through oral fluid supplementation, which may reduce enterohepatic circulation. The objective of this study was to evaluate the risks and benefits of fluid supplementation compared to standard fluid management in term and preterm newborns with unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia undergoing phototherapy. A systematic search was conducted using databases such as CENTRAL, PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL, along with clinical trial registries and conference proceedings, to identify relevant randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized trials. The inclusion criteria were RCTs comparing fluid supplementation to no supplementation or comparing different types of fluid supplementation. Data were extracted using standard Cochrane Neonatal Review Group methods, and the Covidence platform was utilized. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility and risk of bias of the studies. Results were expressed as mean difference (MD), risk difference (RD), and risk ratio (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Out of 1449 articles screened, seven studies were included in the review. Three additional studies were awaiting classification, two of which were completed trials that appeared unpublished. The included studies involved two main comparisons: IV fluid supplementation versus no supplementation (six studies) and IV fluid supplementation versus oral supplementation (one study). A total of 494 term, healthy newborns with unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia were evaluated. The studies were generally at high risk of bias for blinding of care personnel, with unclear risks of bias for blinding of outcome assessors and allocation concealment. The quality of evidence for major outcomes ranged from low to moderate. In the comparison of IV fluid supplementation versus no supplementation, no infants in either group developed bilirubin encephalopathy in the one study that reported this outcome. Serum bilirubin levels were lower at four hours post-intervention in the IV fluid group (MD -34.00 μmol/L or -1.99 mg/dL, 95% CI -52.29 to -15.71; participants = 67; study = 1), but the evidence was of low quality due to indirectness and suspected publication bias. Beyond eight hours post-intervention, serum bilirubin levels were similar between the groups. The duration of phototherapy was significantly shorter in the fluid-supplemented group, but the estimate was affected by unexplained heterogeneity (MD -10.70 hours, 95% CI -15.55 to -5.85; participants = 218; studies = 3; I² = 67%). Fluid-supplemented infants were less likely to require exchange transfusion (RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.71; RD -0.01, 95% CI -0.04 to 0.02; participants = 462; studies = 6; I² = 72%), but this estimate was also affected by heterogeneity and low-quality evidence due to inconsistency and suspected publication bias. Breastfeeding frequencies were similar between fluid-supplemented and non-supplemented infants during the first three days, based on one study (day three estimate: MD 0.90 feeds, 95% CI -0.40 to 2.20; participants = 60), with moderate-quality evidence downgraded for imprecision. In the comparison of IV versus oral fluid supplementation, one study provided all outcome data. No infants in either group developed abnormal neurological signs. Serum bilirubin levels and the rate of change in bilirubin levels were similar between the groups at four hours post-phototherapy (serum bilirubin: MD 11.00 μmol/L or 0.64 mg/dL, 95% CI -21.58 to 43.58; rate of change: MD 0.80 μmol/L/hour or 0.05 mg/dL/hour, 95% CI -2.55 to 4.15; participants = 54 for both outcomes). The quality of evidence for these outcomes was moderate, downgraded for indirectness. The number of infants requiring exchange transfusion was also similar between the groups (RR 1.60, 95% CI 0.60 to 4.27; RD 0.11, 95% CI -0.12 to 0.34; participants = 54). No adverse effects, such as vomiting or abdominal distension, were reported in either group. In conclusion, there is no evidence that IV fluid supplementation impacts critical clinical outcomes such as bilirubin encephalopathy, kernicterus, or cerebral palsy in healthy, term newborns with unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia undergoing phototherapy. None of the infants in the included studies developed these bilirubin-associated complications. Lowto moderate-quality evidence suggests differences in serum bilirubin levels between fluid-supplemented and control groups at certain time points, but the clinical significance of these differences remains unclear. There is no evidence to suggest a difference in efficacy between IV and oral fluid supplementation in reducing serum bilirubin levels. Additionally, no adverse events or complications were associated with fluid supplementation. Future research should focus on populations with higher baseline risks of bilirubin-related neurological complications, such as preterm or low birthweight infants, those with haemolytic hyperbilirubinaemia, or those with dehydration, to evaluate different fluid supplementation regimens.
